## Maximizing the likelihood and numerical methods

- Algebraic maximization of *ln L*(**β**\|**x**,**y**) (i.e., the log-likelihood) is rarely possible
- Numerical methods search for the maximum using the slope and change in slope of the likelihood equation (i.e., first and second derivatives)
  - β estimates correspond to the peak of the log-likelihood curve---when the first derivative = 0
  - Standard error (SE) estimates are largely a function of the rate of change around the β estimate (the top of the curve). This is the second derivative. More peaked distributions will produce smaller SEs (more certainty about β estimate). Flatter distributions will produce larger SEs (less certainty about β estimate)
- Estimates of parameters are usually very close in different software, with perhaps small differences in standard errors

**\*NOTE:** It is more complicated when we have multiple IVs---but this basic intuition about how MLE works with one IV should suffice for the purposes of this class

## Possible problems with ML

- A flat likelihood function makes convergence difficult
- Which curve pictured below would produce smaller SEs?

![](images/ml-curves.png){width=50% fig-alt="Two log-likelihood curves with the same peak at beta-hat: one sharply peaked and one flatter."}

- *Little variation in a DV* or for a given IV can cause problems
- Some models (but not those we consider in this class) can have a *local maxima*

### Maximum Likelihood Estimates

- Under general conditions, the ML estimates are:
  - *Consistent*: The mean of the sampling distribution approaches the true value
  - *Asymptotically efficient*: Data are used as well as possible
  - *Asymptotically normal*: The sampling distribution becomes normal with large samples

## MLE and sample size

- *Consistency*, *normality*, and *efficiency* are asymptotic properties
- OLS tends to work well with very small samples
  - MLE often requires larger samples (but, some bespoke solutions)
  - Should consider both overall size of sample as well as sparseness of the data for what you are modeling
- ML estimators are ***not necessarily bad*** in small samples
  - But small sample behavior is largely unknown

### ML estimators

- Maximum likelihood is an extremely flexible tool for estimating models. As you learn more complex models (e.g., hierarchical models, panel models, latent variable models, structural equation models, etc.) there is a high likelihood (pun!) that the standard practice will be to estimate the model via maximum likelihood
